correctness.rationale: A bijection maps the length-n XOR feedback action to cyclic rotation on the even-parity subspace of F2^(n+1). Fixed-site noise maps to incidence vectors of cycle-graph edges connecting positions j apart. The graph has gcd(j,n+1) components; the first n+1-g edges form a forest, giving exact rank r_t=min(t,n+1-g). Uniform independent fair bits map uniformly onto the rank-r_t affine support, so the total-variation identity is exact. Residue-class parities generate the quotient, and Burnside counting proves the class structure. The stdlib checker passed 186840 orbit-rank, 1039 exact-state law, and 12 cyclic-class-count checks. These finite checks are supplementary, not substitutes for the all-parameter proof.

originality.rationale: The closest fully inspected primary theorem (Levin--Tankala, arXiv:2109.05387, Section 5, Theorem 2) covers the fixed middle site of even-dimensional registers and asserts uniformity at time n. It neither classifies arbitrary fixed sites nor gives a total-variation profile or the nonergodic parity-orbit classes. Diaconis--Graham (1992) proves sharp mixing for a Jordan-block matrix, a different deterministic map; their general affine formulation explains the family but not the cyclic arithmetic rank. Chung--Diaconis--Graham (1987) concerns modular integer affine walks. Searches of mathematical records for the precise gcd criterion and its equivalents found no dominating theorem. General algebraic controllability theory could imply parts of the result, so priority is not certified.

value.rationale: The site of randomness is an intrinsic design choice for the concrete shift-register sampler studied in the cited primary paper. The gcd criterion gives an exact, dimension-independent feasibility condition, detects permanent failure of convergence when violated, supplies all finite-time TV distances, and classifies closed classes and periods. This is a structural positive/negative dichotomy in a natural finite-state probability family, not a routine single numerical example or a minor asymptotic estimate.
